lines.note: Jinbasoo is identified only as a named marine plant; the Portuguese does not establish a botanical species. The opening capital is damaged, while the final caron is visible.
Jinben denotes something rare and marvellous. Italic Vt introduces the example of manifesting such wonders on the following row.
Jinben wo genzuru means performing or manifesting wonders. The Portuguese begins the paired gloss “perform miracles or wonders.”
Marauilhas completes the preceding alternative to milagres; this short Portuguese continuation is a separate physical row.
Jinbenna is the adjectival form, directly glossed as marvellous. It supplies the semantic base for the two unglossed derivatives below.
Jinbenni is the adverbial derivative, “marvellously”; its indentation groups it with Jinbenna rather than with a new Portuguese definition.
Jinbensa is the corresponding abstract noun, marvellousness. The visible long s belongs to the Japanese suffix, not to a Portuguese word.
Jinbita hito describes a mature, dignified person. The Portuguese begins “a grave, modest and cultivated man”; mo- continues into deſto below.
Completes modeſto and adds politico, here describing cultivated manners rather than political activity.
Jinbut is explained through hito and mono and then defined as a person’s appearance or countenance; ſembran- continues below.
Completes ſembrante da peßoa. Jinbut ga yoi illustrates an attractive appearance, with Portuguese parecer divided across the next boundary.
Parecer and fermoſura express good looks or beauty. The next example begins jinbut no yoi hito, retaining its printed fi- division.
To completes hito. Latin l introduces jinbutxa as an alternative designation for a handsome, well-presented man.
Aſombrado completes bem aſombrado, describing a pleasing appearance. The print has a single long s, which is not silently doubled.
Jinbutxa receives a separate entry stating how the term is ordinarily used in conversation; the actual description follows below.

runs.text: por homem de bom parecer, ou bem apeßoado.

lines.note: Completes the conversational definition: a good-looking or well-proportioned man. The damaged first vowel of homem is o, not the OCR’s a.
Jinka is paraphrased as hito no iye, a house inhabited by people. The Japanese paraphrase remains upright.
Jinchi is the knowledge or understanding of a refined, courteous person. The Portuguese abbreviation homẽ is retained without expansion.
Jinkoo is literally people’s mouths; this first homograph introduces an idiom about being talked about. The circumflex is visible.
Jinkoo ni noru means circulating on people’s lips, exactly matching the Portuguese idiom andar nas bocas dos homens.
The second Jinkoo is glossed fukaku atsushi, deeply abundant or great. It is a distinct sense, not a repetition of “mouths.”
Govon jinkoo no itari expresses the exceptional magnitude of received favours. Mui continues as muitos below without a visible terminal hyphen.
Tos completes muitos beneficios, many favours. The final upright S is the dictionary’s written-register label, not part of the italic gloss.
Jinkun, explained as hito kimi, denotes a principal lord. Tono is a Japanese title embedded within the Portuguese explanation.
Jindai is intensively great or extraordinary, as the repeated hanahada paraphrase explains. The scan preserves the initial I omitted by OCR.
Completes grande couſa and adds extraordinary or profound; these are coordinated descriptions of Jindai, not new entries.
Jindaiji denotes the whole earth. The scan separates vôquina chi; retain printed Tçucuru rather than replacing it with a modern expected form.
Ra completes terra, followed by “or the whole world.” This closes the geographical extent gloss of Jindaiji.
Jindei is fukaki doro, deep mud. Atoleiro and lama alta identify a mire or deep muddy ground.
Jinden denotes fields or lands belonging to the kami. Camis is the Japanese religious term with a Portuguese plural ending inside the gloss.

runs.text: Certa laya de frechas de ponta

lines.note: Jindoo is a kind of arrow; Yasaki is the supplied Japanese equivalent. The initial I omitted by OCR is visible, and the blunt point is described below.

runs.text: romba com que tirão aos paſſaros.

lines.note: The arrows have blunt points and are used to shoot birds. This completes the definition without adding a modern weapon classification.
Jinen is explained as occurring of itself or naturally. Per ſi retains the printed historical phrasing.
Jingyoo is paraphrased as ashita too and means early in the morning. The final a of manhaã carries the tilde.
The morning bell awakens the sleep of birth-and-death. The initial mark is a paragraph sign before Iingiǒno, not the OCR’s A.

runs.text: Lib. 4. O ſino que ſe tange antema

lines.note: Feiq. supplies the literary citation; the book number is visibly 4, not a paragraph sign. The translation begins with the bell sounded before dawn.

runs.text: nhaã faz eſpertar a lembrança da morte.

lines.note: Nhaã completes antemanhaã without an added hyphen above. The Portuguese interprets awakening as recalling death; preserve that interpretation rather than rewriting it from the Japanese.
Jingyuu is glossed as deep accumulation or increase. The first letter is I, not F; retain the printed separated a crecentamento and damaged final vowel with caron.
Ou acumulação provides the alternative “or accumulation,” completing the preceding increase gloss.
Jingo, paraphrased through human speaking, is people’s discourse. The final letter of homẽs is s, not the OCR’s t.
The example compares something to a parrot learning human speech. The Japanese Vǒmu and Portuguese He co- retain their physical forms and division.

runs.text: mo papagayo, que fala como homem mas não

lines.note: Completes como and describes the parrot as speaking like a person, but introduces the negative qualification continued below.
Entende o que diz completes “does not understand what it says,” distinguishing imitation of speech from understanding.
The second Jingo is independently glossed as a limit or end; it must not be merged with the preceding speech entry.
Jinguu, explained as kami miya, is a kami shrine. The printed circumflex over u is retained; the final Cami occurs inside Portuguese.
Jingi introduces two moral and social virtues. The scan’s initial I corrects OCR F, and q̃ is an unexpanded abbreviation.

runs.text: os Iapoẽs, & Chinas muito estimão, que ſão

lines.note: The virtues are said to be highly esteemed by Japanese and Chinese people. Their identification continues at the top of column 2.
Continues Jingi from column 1: love and compassion for one’s neighbour are paired with moral propriety; the second description continues below.
Respect or modesty completes the second virtue. Jingi wo mop- begins the example of making these virtues one’s principal concern.
Parato completes mopparato; suru supplies the verb. The Portuguese describes valuing and favouring these virtues, with de- continuing below.
Completes deſtas duas virtudes moraes, referring back to the two virtues rather than introducing another ethical term.
This separate Jingi is concerned with kami, not the moral virtues. Camis is embedded in the Portuguese identification of Japanese divinities.
Sanxu no jingi introduces the three kinds of sacred treasures. This example belongs to a third homographic entry.

runs.text: de couſas precioſas, ou tres peças ricas do Cami.

lines.note: The treasures are described as three kinds of precious objects or rich pieces belonging to the kami; no individual objects are enumerated.

runs.text: Certa dignidade de Cũgues q̃ tem

lines.note: Jingikan is a court office or dignity. The initial Ii sequence is visible; Cũgues names court nobles within the Portuguese, which continues below.

runs.text: ſuperintendencia ſobre as couſas dos Camis.

lines.note: The office supervises affairs of the kami. This relative clause completes the preceding dignity definition.
Iinho is explicitly glossed “second daughter.” The printed nh spelling is retained rather than recast as a modern kinship term.
Jinja is paraphrased as kami no yashiro, a shrine. The initial I lost by OCR is visible; the Portuguese complement follows below.
Camis completes “house or shrine of the kami.” This one-word body continuation remains separate from the following headword.
Jinji denotes ceremonies and festivals of the kami. The initial is I rather than F, and the gloss ends festas rather than OCR festis.
Dos Camis completes the ritual definition. Camis is part of the Portuguese clause, not a standalone Japanese synonym.
Jinjin expresses exceptional depth or magnitude. The scan supplies initial Ii and a comma after grande, connecting the following alternative.
Jinjin no chijin illustrates deep friendship. The visible ending is chijin, not chiju; Grã- begins the Portuguese “great friend.”
Completes grande amigo and begins jinjin no govon, great favours received from a respected person. Gran- continues below.

runs.text: des beneficios recebidos de peßoa alta.

lines.note: Completes grandes beneficios and specifies that they are received from a person of high standing.

runs.text: Septimo dia dos primeiros do Xǒguachi.

lines.note: Jinjit names the seventh day of the first month. The mark in the embedded Xǒguachi is a caron, not the OCR’s tilde.
Jinin is paraphrased through compassion and endurance, with Portuguese piedade beginning the paired abstract gloss.
Paciencia supplies the second virtue, patience. The final upright S labels written usage and is distinct from the italic gloss.
Jinjoo is decorum, modesty and gravity. Policia here concerns polished conduct rather than a modern police institution.
Jinjoona is the corresponding adjective, refined and modest. The example starts Iin at the edge without a supplied hyphen.
Completes jinjoona hito, a modest and honourable person. The scan supports initial h in honeſto, not OCR b; the description continues below.
Suas acçoens completes the description of a person who is modest and honourable in his actions.
Jinjooni is the adverbial derivative, referring to acting with decorum. Its printed indentation connects it with Jinjoona.
Jinjoosa is the abstract noun for the corresponding decorum or modesty; the caron and long s are preserved.
Jinme, kami no uma, is a horse belonging to a kami. The final Cami is embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Jinmet denotes complete destruction, paraphrased through exhaustion and perishing. The final upright S marks written usage.
Jinmiaku is the pulse associated with the kidneys in the dictionary’s medical terminology. The gloss reports that association without anatomical elaboration.

runs.text: Eternidade, ou tempo que eſtà por

lines.note: Jinmiraisai denotes eternity or limitless future time. The Portuguese relative clause continues below; the edge context confirms por is complete.
Completes “infinite time to come.” Upright S is the written-register label rather than part of the italic phrase.
Jinmit is something very secret. The following upright S is a usage label, not an additional word of the definition.
Jinmoo is hito no nozomi, people’s desire. The Portuguese noun homens divides at the visible ho- ending.
Mens completes homens, closing the collective-desire gloss; the final S is upright.
Jinmon is hito no kado, a person’s gate or house-front. The first character is I, not long s; fronteſpi- continues below.
Completes fronteſpicio da caſa de alguem, the front of someone’s house. The word remains divided at the physical line break.

runs.text: Homens, & as de mais couſas do

lines.note: Jinmot collectively denotes people and the other things of the world. Preserve the printed separated de mais.
Mundo completes the preceding expression “of the world”; this is a genuine one-word body continuation.
Jin muhen is boundlessness or immensity. The scan retains a space after Iin and an f in mufen; S is upright.
Jinmuryoo is equated with the preceding immensity gloss. The initial is a descending lowercase j, not OCR r; its lowercase form is retained.
Jinnin, kami no hito, denotes people serving the kami. The final preposition is aos, not OCR aoe, and both abbreviation tildes remain unexpanded.
Jin no fu is equated with hookoo and glossed “bladder.” Restore the scan’s initial I and retain the historical Portuguese Bixiga.
Jinpan begins with the figurative image of a many-coloured man and then clarifies it as a malicious person. The explanatory i has a comma.
The proverb contrasts a tiger’s visible markings with human duplicity. Its second compound jin-pan is divided across this row and the next.
Completes jinpan wa miegatashi, human duplicity being hard to discern. Xix. is an upright citation label; the Portuguese begins “the spotted tiger.”

runs.text: do logo ſe deixa ver, mas o homem malicioſo não

lines.note: Do completes malhado. The tiger is readily visible, but the malicious person is not understood; the edge shows full não without a hyphen.
Completes não ha quẽ o entenda: no one understands the malicious person. OCR grouped this body continuation with the separate catchword Iinpi.; both are now represented separately.
